### **Section 1**

<!-- ¶2 -->
_Driving efficiency, ensuring compliance, and extending asset life — JC Solutions offers the value, innovation, and commitment to help the County meet today’s needs while preparing for tomorrow’s challenges. Our team is equipped with next-level O&M tools and strategies designed to elevate daily operations, reduce costs, and protect your capital investments by extending the life of existing and new assets. We bring a long-standing track record of regulatory compliance, with a history of meeting and exceeding permit requirements across multiple jurisdictions. Our partnership model is rooted in transparency and backed by a deep bench of local and national resources, enabling rapid reach-back for expert support and continuous improvement. We’ve successfully deployed advanced technologies that competitors only aspire to, and our in-house membrane bioreactor (MBR), SCADA, and system optimization experts are just a phone call away._

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **WE’RE MORE THAN AN OPERATOR: WE’RE YOUR STRATEGIC PARTNER FOR WASTEWATER EXCELLENCE & COMPLIANCE**

<!-- ¶4 -->
Jacobs and Atlanta-based, minority-owned firm CERM have formed a joint venture, JC Solutions (A Jacobs/CERM JV), to deliver compliant operations and maintenance services for wastewater facilities and pump stations in the North Fulton County. This joint venture is a natural evolution of our partnership and a perfect alignment of complementary strengths. Built on over 20 years of combined experience across water, education, aviation, and transportation projects, our partnership brings together complementary strengths: Jacobs’ deep O&M expertise and national best practices, and CERM’s strong local presence, workforce development programs, and community partnerships. Jacobs is the only fully integrated O&M firm in North America—U.S.-based, Fortune 500, and built for stability. With $12 billion in FY24 revenue and a $2.4 billion O&M backlog, we bring unmatched scale and staying power. Our 4,000+ U.S. O&M professionals and 45,000 global staff make us the industry’s largest and most diverse operations partner. CERM was founded in 1995 as a minority-owned engineering, environmental, and program management consulting firm, and has grown into an awardwinning organization with 100+ professionals serving the southeastern U.S. CERM offers robust workforce development programs and strong local and regional partnerships. Together, we bring a shared commitment to regulatory compliance, environmental stewardship, and operational excellence.

<!-- ¶5 -->
**By combining Jacobs’ national technical leadership with CERM’s deep local roots and capacity-building expertise, we are uniquely positioned to deliver consistently compliant and reliable services, optimize life cycle costs, and maintain Fulton County’s (County) assets to the highest standards.**

**OUR SOLUTION IS COMPREHENSIVE, FOCUSED ON REGULATORY COMPLIANCE, OPTIMIZATION AND ASSET PRESERVATION, AND DELIVERS VALUE TODAY AND TOMORROW**

<!-- ¶2 -->
JC Solutions delivers a comprehensive O&M strategy grounded in deep expertise across MBR systems, asset management, and process optimization. Our partnership with Fulton County is built on a foundation of exceptional regulatory compliance— and so much more. We bring a forward-looking vision powered by advanced digital tools, intelligent O&M platforms, and data-driven decision-making that optimize performance and manage costs. Backed by Jacobs’ extensive technical resources and CERM’s strong local presence and workforce development leadership, we are fully committed to safeguarding the County’s infrastructure and serving the community well into the future.

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### Key features and benefits of our solution for Fulton County include:

<!-- ¶4 -->
Meaningful Partnership Built on Transparency, Accountability and Investment in Community. Our approach is grounded in transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement—the same model that has driven a 98% client renewal rate across our portfolio. We will work side by side with the County to tackle operational challenges, implement innovative O&M strategies, and proactively plan for the future. Beyond plant operations, we’re committed to community engagement—expanding on the successful outreach at the Johns Creek Environmental Campus and partnering with the Chattahoochee Nature Center to deliver impactful education programs that foster the next generation of water stewards.

<!-- ¶5 -->
Proven Regulatory Compliance and Environmental Stewardship. With a 99.98% compliance rate across hundreds of regulated facilities, our track record speaks for itself. We will apply our rigorous internal audit protocols and QA/QC processes to ensure full compliance at all three of the County’s facilities—integrating proactive sampling, noise and odor mitigation, and continuous monitoring to meet all EPA, Georgia EPD, and County standards.

<!-- ¶6 -->
Expert Staff, Locally Grounded and Regionally Backed. Our team includes highly qualified, licensed professionals with deep knowledge of advanced wastewater technologies, pump station operations, and the unique complexities of the Fulton County system. Many have direct experience at Big Creek and JCEC, bringing valuable institutional knowledge. They’re supported by Jacobs’ unmatched regional network of 1,200+ Georgia-based staff—offering expertise in SCADA, MBR optimization, capital planning, commissioning, and more.

<!-- ¶7 -->
MBR Experience and Expertise to Protect and Maximize Your Return on Investment. Our global and Atlanta-based MBR experts—like Scott Levesque, PE, and Youngchui Choi, PE—provide deep handson knowledge in MBR system design and operations. From membrane life extension and optimized chemical dosing to enhanced effluent quality, we offer proven, practical solutions that protect the County’s investment while delivering performance that meets the highest operational and public expectations.

<!-- ¶8 -->
Seamless Transition with Proven Talent Retention. We understand the value of continuity and staff retention during transition. Led by Transition Manager Mike Boven—who uniquely brings experience with both Jacobs and Veolia—we are equipped to manage a smooth, informed transition that eliminates disruptions and preserves institutional knowledge. Our recent transitions of Veolia-operated sites this past year in MA, MS, and CA involving over 100 FTEs illustrate our ability to deliver rapid, successful handovers without compromising service quality.

<!-- ¶9 -->
Fresh Perspectives Paired with Advanced Technologies for Elevated O&M. We bring a revitalized team equipped with fresh perspectives and cutting-edge tools. Through Intelligent O&M, Replica™, and an ISO 55001-aligned Asset Management Program, we will optimize asset performance, improve maintenance efficiency, and reduce costs. Our use of advanced analytics, SCADA integration, and predictive modeling empowers real-time decision-making while safeguarding long-term infrastructure value.

<!-- ¶10 -->
Workforce Development that Builds Local Capacity. Workforce stability starts with investment. We provide structured training, career development, and certification incentives to retain and grow local talent. Our partner, CERM, enhances this through community-based workforce programs that strengthen the County’s labor pipeline and support long-term operational resilience.

<!-- ¶11 -->
Over $6.7 Million in Added Value from Day One. Our base proposal includes more than $6.7 million in digital tools, technical resources, and innovation investments—delivering immediate and lasting value to the County. These enhancements are designed to improve service delivery, extend asset life, and keep costs down—without increasing the County’s budget.

<!-- ¶12 -->
Exclusive Consulting Discount Adds Immediate Value. As part of our commitment to long-term partnership and cost transparency, Jacobs is offering Fulton County an exclusive discounted rate structure for consulting services directly tied to our O&M work at the North Fulton wastewater facilities. This discount allows the County to access Jacobs’ top-tier engineering and technical expertise—such as follow-up studies from our Annual Innovation Workshops—at significantly reduced rates.

###### **APPROACH ROOTED IN PROJECT UNDERSTANDING, ALIGNED WITH COUNTY OBJECTIVES, AND READY TO TACKLE POTENTIAL CHALLENGES HEAD-ON**

<!-- ¶3 -->
Membrane management will be a top priority. With fouling recognized as one of the greatest risks to system performance, we will apply our deep expertise in Kubota and Zenon membrane systems to extend membrane life, reduce cleaning frequency, and optimize process control—protecting the County’s investment while ensuring high effluent quality and reliability.

<!-- ¶4 -->
JC Solutions brings deep familiarity with the North Fulton wastewater facilities, reinforced by firsthand operational experience and a clear understanding of each plant’s strengths, challenges, and future needs. Our insights stem from recent site visits, direct work at these and other facilities, and validation with Kubota’s research and reference installations. Several members of our proposed team have operated or supported Big Creek, JCEC, and Little River firsthand— bringing invaluable institutional knowledge to the County’s operations.

<!-- ¶5 -->
Our site visits also revealed opportunities for improved maintenance and equipment reliability as well as enhanced safety and housekeeping practices. We will act swiftly to address these issues—prioritizing operational safety, facility appearance, and asset stewardship.

<!-- ¶6 -->
While Fulton County has demonstrated a strong commitment to regulatory compliance and maintaining high aesthetic standards— particularly at the Johns Creek Environmental Campus—recent compliance exceedances under the current O&M provider underscore the urgent need for a more proactive, accountable, and transparent operational approach. Our team will immediately implement

Our history working with Fulton County facilities provides us with unique insights into these three sophisticated MBR plants. ###### **LITTLE RIVER PLANT**

<!-- ¶7 -->
The County is completing an upgrade to 32 MGD (max month average) for this MBR plant, designed with future expansion capability to 38 MGD. The facility utilizes a comprehensive treatment process including screening, grit removal, primary clarification, biological nutrient removal, membrane filtration, UV disinfection, and post-aeration before discharge to the Chattahoochee River.

<!-- ¶8 -->
This 15 MGD (max month average) MBR plant features aesthetically-pleasing design elements to blend with surrounding high-value residential areas. The facility utilizes Kubota membranes and includes innovative design elements such as a self-cleaning trench-style pump station. The plant discharges to the Chattahoochee River and is located in close proximity to a water intake facility.

<!-- ¶9 -->
This smaller facility rated at 2.6 MGD (annual average capacity) currently operates at approximately 0.8 MGD. The plant was converted from a conventional oxidation ditch system to an MBR process, repurposing existing structures including oxidation ditches for bioreactors and former clarifiers for post-anoxic zones. Unlike the other facilities, this plant is physically located in Cherokee County but serves Fulton County.

## Page 20

<!-- ¶1 -->
###### **_Planned Improvements to Meet Future Needs_**

<!-- ¶2 -->
The County places high priority on permit compliance with substantial safety margins, particularly for phosphorus removal, even when this approach requires additional chemical usage and expense. There are plans to expand JCEC from 15 to 20 MGD, with a design-build team currently evaluating options. For Big Creek, the future plans to expand from 32 to 38 MGD capacity would require adding a primary clarifier, a bioreactor, and more membranes. The County is also considering a biosolids disposal project at Big Creek, potentially involving drying or other processing technologies.

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Key Current and Future Challenges_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
Our understanding includes insights into critical challenges faced by the facilities, which briefly note below. We provided more detailed discussion of these challenges and our approach to providing solutions under each of these topics covered later in this section.

<!-- ¶5 -->
**Staffing/Workforce:** Throughout the wastewater O&M industry, there are significant challenges in hiring and retaining qualified and certified staff, and the North Fulton facilities are not immune to these issues. Additionally, training and motivating a high performing workforce requires a culture that values these important components of a comprehensive O&M delivery approach.

<!-- ¶6 -->
**Odor Control:** The JCEC facility has experienced odor complaints from nearby residents. The plant was designed with special attention to aesthetics and odor control due to proximity to expensive homes. All plants have odor control systems, with Johns Creek and Big Creek utilizing chemical scrubbers and GAC, while Little River uses GAC alone for its headworks. Operations must meet odor control requirements.

<!-- ¶7 -->
**Biosolids Management:** Little River's biosolids are hauled to Big Creek for processing. A key challenge at Big Creek is the lack of dedicated thickening processes for primary sludge and waste activated sludge, which limits dewatering efficiency and increases disposal costs. Future plans may include a drying facility at Big Creek, where there is available real estate from demolished sand filters.

<!-- ¶8 -->
**Membrane Operations:** The North Fulton facilities face several optimization challenges including membrane performance management.

<!-- ¶9 -->
<!-- Start of picture text -->

<!-- ¶10 -->
Big Creek has new Kubota flat plates, Little River's hollow fiber membranes are six years old, and JCEC's are 16 years old, which is well past expected life, requiring imminent replacement. All three plants use enhanced biological phosphorus removal and present opportunities for improvement in operations. Chemical optimization opportunities also exist across the facilities, particularly in correctly dosing sodium hypochlorite and sodium hydroxide for the chemical scrubbers at Big Creek and JCEC (saving approximately $500/day), proper Phos-Zorb application, and addressing the significant under-provision of sodium hydroxide for alkalinity at Little River.

communication practices—we commit to regular operations meetings, proactive issue notifications, and open-door access to our management team. <!-- ¶10 -->
Providing high-quality, compliant O&M services is part of our company’s DNA—not a trend or transitional strategy subject to ownership changes or shifting priorities. ###### **ENERGY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY**

<!-- ¶7 -->
JC Solutions will develop a comprehensive Energy Management Strategy for the North Fulton wastewater facilities and associated pump stations. Our approach goes beyond traditional energy efficiency measures to identify significant cost-saving opportunities through strategic rate structure optimization, demand management, and innovative operational strategies.

<!-- ¶8 -->
###### **_Comprehensive Rate Structure Analysis_**

<!-- ¶9 -->
Our team will conduct a detailed review of current electricity rate structures for all three treatment plants and 28 pump stations within the Fulton County system. We will model electric utility costs across all relevant Georgia Power rate structures to identify least-cost options for each facility, taking into account the unique operational characteristics of each site. By analyzing historical consumption patterns, we can determine significant opportunities for rate optimization and identify facilities where alternative rate classifications could yield immediate savings without capital investment.

<!-- ¶10 -->
###### **_Strategic Demand Management_**

<!-- ¶11 -->
JC Solutions will develop facility-specific strategies to reduce peak demand charges across the North Fulton facilities. Our approach includes modeling backup generator deployment for strategic peak shaving, with careful consideration of emissions thresholds and noise constraints to ensure regulatory compliance and community harmony. We will evaluate battery energy storage systems (BESS) for peak demand reduction through detailed financial feasibility analysis that considers current rates and future projections. For viable energy asset deployments, we will create automated control strategies that optimize battery charging/discharging cycles aligned with rate structures and operational needs.

<!-- ¶12 -->
###### **_Georgia Power Partnership_**

<!-- ¶13 -->
Leveraging our established relationship with Georgia Power, JC Solutions can negotiate preferred rate classifications for the North Fulton facilities to maximize cost savings. Our team will coordinate directly with utility representatives to identify interconnection requirements for any proposed energy assets, ensuring smooth implementation of recommended solutions. Georgia Power's tariff structures are notably complex and often require active daily or hourly management to optimize—a capability our

###### **_Maintenance Planner/Scheduler Powered by Palantir_**

<!-- ¶16 -->
Managing limited maintenance resources, both labor and materials, is a major focus for the team, and getting it right makes a big difference with preserving assets and meeting budget. Most existing computerized maintenance management systems (CMMS) can only store work orders

<!-- ¶17 -->
and asset information, but they do not have any way to optimize the priorities of work orders for the maintenance team. This becomes a laborintensive process by the maintenance planner/scheduler or maintenance manager.

<!-- ¶18 -->
Instead, Jacobs has developed a very unique support tool that is an overlay on top of any CMMS that makes optimal use of limited maintenance resources (labor and parts) to maximize KPIs and also drive down costs. The most direct way to optimize maintenance resources is through proper planning and scheduling, but the procedures are extensive and complex and require a planner/scheduler or maintenance manager to hold several, often competing, metrics or variables in mind simultaneously. This is unrealistic for most people unless they have many years of experience and a very strong understanding of asset management theory.

<!-- ¶4 -->
The latest module added to the Intelligent O&M suite of tools uses large language model (LLM) AI on the Palantir Foundry platform to ingest and read only a specific plant’s documentation and give users a search engine style interface to ask plain English questions and get answers in seconds. First deployed at our project at the Spokane County, WA, Regional WWTP, the system is designed to only use site-specific information, but in any format—CMMS, electronic manuals, PDF files, Word documents, scanned documents, CAD drawings, etc. The AI Assistant ( **Exhibit 2-8** ) only uses this library for answering questions, and nothing is obtained from the internet unless it is specifically related to what the maintenance team wants to know.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **_Maintenance AI Assistant Powered by Palantir_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
Wastewater treatment facilities have thousands of assets, and nearly every one of them comes with an equipment manual that defines what type of lubricant, repair parts, preventive maintenance, and other details are critical to maximizing the life of the asset. Much of this essential, frequently needed information like maintenance schedules, will be built into the CMMS. The maintenance team will still need to regularly refer to the vendor manuals, each being possibly hundreds of pages in length. Combined with the total number of assets, a mechanic might be faced with finding a needle in a haystack of information on a random shelf where plant documents are kept. The same kind of sorting problem happens when looking at equipment repair histories in CMMS —tools to support mechanics with this kind of plant-specific information have been unavailable. **Until now.**

<!-- ¶7 -->
Our maintenance teams are now able to access vast stores of their own information at incredible speed. Questions like, “What are the safety concerns when working with the microturbine?” are answered with a few summary bullets, and then the reference pages are listed and linked showing exactly where the information came from. This is a vital step in building trust in the validity of the results. Other broader questions are even more exciting, such as “What five pumps require the most maintenance based on work order history since 2017?” or “List the top ten

AquaDNA: Smart Technology for System Optimization<br>While the collections system beyond the pump stations is not part of the<br>scope of services for this contract, we recognize that overflows present<br>significant management challenges that can lead to compliance issues and<br>operational inefficiencies, especially during wet weather events. To address<br>these challenges, we’re including Jacobs’ Palantir-driven AquaDNA tools as<br>part of our comprehensive solution for North Fulton facilities.<br>AquaDNA uses smart technology and sensors for wastewater collection<br>systems to understand performance in real time, alert operators to potential<br>incidents, and help avoid spills, floods, overflows, and backups that could<br>harm customers and the environment. While wet weather is primarily<br>managed through the collection system—with wet weather management<br>tanks only becoming available at Big Creek after construction completion—<br>AquaDNA offers an immediate solution by visualizing pump station<br>operations, monitoring critical sewer levels, and providing predictive alarms.<br>Our offering integrates near real-time data from multiple County systems<br>onto the AquaDNA platform, powered by Palantir’s Foundry. <!-- ¶4 -->
###### ABOVE AND BEYOND **VALUE-ADDED EXTRAS**

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### AQUADNA SMART SYSTEM OPTIMIZATION

<!-- ¶6 -->
Our AquaDNA solution delivers comprehensive protection against costly overflows and system failures through real-time monitoring and predictive analytics powered by Palantir’s Foundry platform. JC Solutions’ investment includes annual licensing costs, equipment/installation for automatic deragging devices at four vulnerable pump stations, flow and level measurement instrumentation, and ongoing calibration and optimization by JC Solutions experts. The system’s dynamic waveform monitoring technology proactively implements pump reversals upon detection of flow or power changes—a unique approach proven across nearly 100 U.S. installations that dramatically reduces emergency callouts, decreases power consumption, extends equipment life, and prevents sanitary sewer overflows. By integrating SCADA information, rain gauge data, level sensors, and weather forecasts, our machine learning algorithms continuously optimize pump station setpoints, transforming raw data into actionable intelligence that enhances operational efficiency and maximizes system performance.

<!-- ¶7 -->
###### $1,663,000 **WORTH OF INVESTMENT BY JC SOLUTIONS**

<!-- ¶8 -->
Additional value will be realized through AquaDNA’s advanced features that encompass broader elements of the collection system. These enhancements include real-time optimization of pump station and diversion level setpoints using sophisticated machine learning methods that adapt to changing system conditions—transforming data into actionable intelligence that enhances operational efficiency and maximizes system performance.

###### **GUIDING PRINCIPLES**

<!-- ¶3 -->
At the heart of our approach is a robust O&M program focused on delivering safe, compliant, and reliable service while protecting and extending the life of Fulton County’s infrastructure. We take a comprehensive view of O&M—one that integrates performance optimization, regulatory compliance, proactive asset management, and stakeholder engagement.

<!-- ¶4 -->
JC Solutions’ operations strategy is driven by data-informed reliability and reinforced through advanced tools like Maintenance Connection, the CMMS software. As a recognized leader in Intelligent O&M, we bring proven opportunities to reduce chemical use, lower energy consumption, and optimize maintenance activities across complex utility systems. With more than 40 years of award-winning O&M experience, JC Solutions blends deep technical resources with practical, day-to-day operational know-how to deliver measurable results. We remain grounded in the fundamentals that define operational excellence—safety, responsiveness, reliability, sustainability, and transparency.

<!-- ¶5 -->
Our delivery model is guided by clearly defined principles and performance expectations, summarized in **Exhibit 2-11** . These principles are reinforced through close collaboration between onsite staff, regional management, and JC Solutions’ nationwide network of subject matter experts. Our operations teams are supported rather than siloed and benefit from access to best practices, technical guidance, and real-time support.

<!-- ¶6 -->
JC Solutions also applies a structured audit and performance review program across all our O&M projects. This includes regularly scheduled audits that assess hundreds of operational tasks, benchmark against historical performance and peer facilities, and generate actionable insights. The results are used to identify trends, prevent performance dips, and promote continuous improvement.

<!-- ¶7 -->
We recognize that the Facilities Plans outlined in **Exhibit E** serve as a foundation for strong operational performance and shared success. JC Solutions will provide a comprehensive discussion of each required plan within the Approach section of this proposal. While some plan

These include but are not limited to Emergency Response, O&M, Staffing, Equipment Performance Testing, and Public Outreach. Each plan is based on Jacobs’ national experience and tailored to the needs of the North Fulton Service Area.

<!-- ¶9 -->
We are fully committed to working in close collaboration with the County to refine and finalize each plan. All plans will be submitted in both electronic and hard copy formats, in full alignment with Exhibit E expectations.

###### **STAFFING PLAN**

<!-- ¶2 -->
Our approach to delivery of the management, operations, and maintenance services of the County’s facilities focuses on high-caliber leadership, reliability, compliance, and efficiency. In **_Section 3: Project Team Qualifications, Qualifications of Key Personnel_** , we discuss our team’s overall organization ( **Exhibit 3-1** ), roles, and identified key personnel. In this section, we discuss our staffing approach for the County’s facilities, including a summary of the total proposed staff (shown in **Exhibit 2-13** ) and shift schedules. Our staffing approach includes all of the required positions in the RFP, and we anticipate offering current qualified staff positions with JC Solutions. We discuss our approach to transitioning current staff later in **_Section 2.9 Transition Plan with Approach and Timeline of Activities Necessary to Achieve the Commencement Date_** .

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Summary Of Delivery Staffing Approach_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
- µ<sup>**Management, administrative and safety staff**</sup> will work eight-hour shifts, Monday through Friday, as shown in **Exhibit 2-14** . We will have two Administrative Assistants who will provide dayto-day support to the project, one located at Big Creek and the other at JCEC. A Health & Safety Specialist will also be located onsite full-time and be responsible for all the the County’s facilities.

<!-- ¶5 -->
- µ<sup>**Big Creek WRF operations staff**will be overseen</sup> day-to-day by the Plant Manager, who will work eight-hour shifts, Monday through Friday. (See **Exhibit 2-15** .) There will be two groups of dayshift operators who will all work 12-hour shifts. A Main Lead Operator along with two Operators will work a total of seven days across two weeks, covering three days during the first week and four days the next week. Similarly, a Secondary

<!-- ¶6 -->
Lead Operator and two Operators will also work shifts across two weeks, and their shifts will cover the four days in the first week and the three days in the second week not covered by the Main Lead Operator group. This ensures three day-shift Operators onsite every day of the week. For night shifts, we will have two groups, each consisting of one Lead Operator and one Operator. They will follow the same shift patterns across two weeks as the two day-shift groups. This ensures two Operators are onsite every night shift of the week.

<!-- ¶7 -->
- µ<sup>**JCEC operations staff**will be overseen day-to-day</sup> by the Plant Manager, who will work eight-hour shifts, Monday through Friday. (See **Exhibit 2-16** .) Lead Operators and Operations will work 12-hour shifts and will follow the same shift patterns as at Big Creek WRF, ensuring the required minimum staffing of three Operators during day shifts and two Operators during night shifts for every day of the week.

<!-- ¶8 -->
µ<sup>**Little River WRF operations staff**will be overseen</sup> day-to-day by the Plant Manager, who will work eight-hour shifts, Monday through Friday. (See **Exhibit 2-17** .) Two day-shift Lead Operators alternate overlapping schedules, blending shorter shifts of 4 or 8 hours with longer 12-hour shifts to maintain daily supervisory coverage. Four day-shift Operators work rotating 12-hour shifts, typically structured to provide consecutive days of work followed by multiple off days. Similarly, two night-shift Lead Operators alternate overnight supervision, each paired closely with a night-shift Operators who mirror their rotation, working 12-hour shifts with alternating days on and off. This shift pattern provides balanced staffing at the smaller Little River WRF while ensuring a minimum of three day shift operators and two night-shift Operators seven days per week.

Jacobs’ Together Beyond global strategy creates a culture of inclusion and belonging where we all thrive by embracing many perspectives— **critical elements to building a culture that retains talent.** Its four strategic pillars are: promoting business growth through different perspectives, building cultural awareness and engagement, developing the best talent, and leadership commitment and accountability. Our vision is to foster fairness and respect for all people, value the differences and similarities in backgrounds and skills, and maximize everyone’s potential.

<!-- ¶3 -->

These groups provide peer support, career development, and mentoring, and raise awareness through discussion groups and activities open to all. Each group has a senior executive sponsor to guide and reinforce the importance of their efforts and to mentor staff who may not otherwise have access to senior leadership.

Jacobs is also actively involved with the Hispanic Engineer National Achievement Awards Corporation, the National Society of Black Engineers, the Society for Hispanic Professional Engineers, the Women’s Transportation Seminar, and the Society of Women Engineers.

###### CROSS-TRAINING FOR CAREER DEVELOPMENT

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Wastewater Operator Certification and Renewal Training_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
Jacobs has developed its own wastewater operations training content through our Institute of Learning platform, covering a wide range of topics but generally aligned to the national Association of Boards of Certification (ABC) “Need to Know” set of standards per certification grade level. These classes were developed with the combined expertise of our operators and engineers, and provided through classroom, field, and online teaching methods. Online quizzes are used to allow students to demonstrate their learning, specific for each subject area. The intent is to improve the skills and competency of our operations staff and support their career growth. Providing training for operators developed by operators is an effective way to accomplish this.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **_Maintenance Training_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
JC Solutions’ approach to maintenance skills training and predictive maintenance techniques improves uptime and reduces corrective maintenance:

<!-- ¶7 -->
- µ<sup>**Certified Maintenance Reliability Technician (CMRT)**exam opportunities at least once a year</sup> for all maintenance staff.

<!-- ¶8 -->
- µ<sup>**Hands-on, in-person instruction for vibration analysis, alignment, oil analysis, CMMS**</sup> **best practices, ultrasound, and troubleshooting.** This is taught by our regional maintenance experts in each subject area.

<!-- ¶9 -->
- µ<sup>**Skills training**—from basic mechanic-in-training to advanced predictive maintenance</sup> training—supports continuous improvement of staff skills and maintenance processes.

<!-- ¶10 -->
Our commitment to these programs has resulted in Jacobs employing more CMRT-certified maintenance staff than any other water/wastewater service provider in the U.S.

<!-- ¶11 -->

<!-- ¶12 -->
JC Solutions is committed to building and sustaining a high-performing operations team at the County’s facilities. Through ongoing professional development, workforce partnerships, and a dedicated staffing strategy, we ensure operators are prepared, empowered, and supported at every stage of their careers.

###### **_Fermentation Zones_**

<!-- ¶9 -->
Fermentation is used at all three plants to create conditions amenable to enhanced biological phosphorus removal (EBPR). Successful EBPR allows the effluent phosphorus limit to be met using the least amount of metal salt (Phos-Zorb, in this case). Best performance is achieved by limiting oxygen and nitrate input to the fermentation zone, which can be evaluated by process simulation. Performance can be further enhanced by starting and stopping mixers to store more solids in the zone.

<!-- ¶10 -->
At Big Creek WRF, the fermentation process is affected by several interrelated operational decisions. First, the fermentation process can be operated with one, two, or three tanks in series ( **Exhibit 2-23** ). Second, the flow rate of its two inputs can be adjusted—fine screen effluent (FSE) and return activated sludge (RAS). Third, the two mixers in each tank can be cycled on and off to allow biomass to accumulate on the floor.

###### **_Swing Zones_**

<!-- ¶2 -->
Big Creek WRF and JCEC include swing zones in their bioreactors, meaning these zones can be aerated or mixed. Several considerations affect the decision of whether to aerate a swing zone, and this is best evaluated using process simulation.

<!-- ¶3 -->
- µ<sup>When a swing zone is aerated, it operates as an aerobic zone. When</sup> aeration is needed to meet effluent ammonia limits (for example, during the winter), it overrides all other considerations.

<!-- ¶4 -->
- µ<sup>When a swing zone is unaerated, it operates as an anoxic zone. Anoxic</sup> zones degrade organic matter using nitrate rather than oxygen, and this decreases aeration requirements and energy consumption of the overall process. It also recovers alkalinity, which decreases chemical use. In general, a swing zone should be unaerated when not needed to meet ammonia limits.

<!-- ¶5 -->
- µ<sup>However, allowing nitrate to reach zero in an anoxic zone works against</sup> EBPR, which is used at all three plants. (Reaching zero nitrate without VFA present results in secondary phosphorus release, which breaks the phosphorus release/uptake cycle.) At JCEC, this can be prevented by providing sufficient internal mixed liquor recycle (IMLR) pumping.

<!-- ¶6 -->
If insufficient pumping capacity exists, it would be necessary to aerate the swing zone. Big Creek WRF does not have IMLR, but RAS flow can be increased to deliver more nitrate to the anoxic zone.

<!-- ¶7 -->
At Big Creek WRF, there is a nitrate probe in the anoxic zone just upstream of the swing zone ( **Exhibit 2-25** ). When the swing zone is unaerated (making it anoxic), it would be ideal to make the nitrate measurement in the swing zone.

###### **_Sodium Hydroxide for Alkalinity Addition at Little River WRF_**

<!-- ¶5 -->
Monthly reports include influent data for BOD and TSS but lack data for total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN), ammonia, and alkalinity. While historical measurements are those required by the NPDES permit, there is insufficient information on which to base process simulations using historical wastewater characteristics. Using the original design basis for TKN, ammonia, and alkalinity, process simulation indicates that far more sodium hydroxide would be required for alkalinity addition (82 gal./ MG) than is reimbursable (6 gal./MG). Our figure already considers the sodium hydroxide contained in Phos-Zorb. In fact, high historical usage of Phos-Zorb at this plant suggests that the incumbent may be overfeeding Phos-Zorb for alkalinity addition, which is not a cost-effective operating strategy.

<!-- ¶6 -->
###### **_Maintaining Good Mixed Liquor Filterability_**

<!-- ¶7 -->
While sludge settleability is not important to an MBR process, mixed liquor filterability is because it’s affected by operation of the biological process, especially temperature and solids retention time (SRT). Longer SRT is needed at lower temperature to ensure adequate removal of organic foulants ( **Exhibit 2-28** ). In addition, the best filterability is achieved when surface wasting is practiced.

<!-- ¶8 -->
JCEC is designed for effective surface wasting, with mixed liquor from all bioreactors passing the foam wasting pump station before it splits to the membrane tanks. Wasting can also be done from RAS, which is at a higher concentration. While surface wasting is beneficial to plant housekeeping (by avoiding foam) and membrane performance (by improving filterability), sludge wasting from RAS is beneficial to dewatering because higher dewatering feed concentration may increase cake concentration and reduce disposal costs. We plan to begin plant operation in the same manner as the incumbent and gradually shift toward surface wasting, ultimately finding the best balance between the two wasting locations.

JCEC does not have this feature, and we would like to discuss with the County the possibility of adding them.

###### **_Reducing Real-Time/Peak Power Consumption_**

<!-- ¶3 -->
The cost of electrical power varies with season and time of day. The cost is highest on summer days, when regional air conditioning places the greatest demands on power supply ( **Exhibit 2-31** ). In addition, most institutional customers’ power bills reflect a peak instantaneous power draw for the year.

<!-- ¶4 -->
###### **_Maximizing Equipment Availability and Treatment Capacity_**

<!-- ¶5 -->
Most equipment systems include a standby process unit. Our approach to preventative maintenance is to strive to achieve 99.98% uptime, including standby units. As a result, each unit process usually will have more than rated capacity, allowing higher flows to be treated, and decreasing the likelihood of collection system overflows. Of course, higher than design peak flows would not be processed if effluent compliance were jeopardized.

<!-- ¶6 -->
The fine screens at JCEC and Big Creek warrant special attention, as they are the final barrier protecting the membranes from damage by debris. Center-fed band screens like those at JCEC experience gradually wear of the bottom seals until the opening at the seals exceeds the opening of the media (two millimeters). For this screen type, it is necessary to remove equipment from the channel to inspect bottom seals. Horizontal drum screens like those at Big Creek also have seals, but they are not located at the bottom and can be easily inspected at deck level. JC Solutions will carefully follow the manufacturers’ recommendations for seal inspection and maintenance.

JCEC uses inline flow equalization, which means water levels in the membrane tanks, bioreactors, and primary clarifiers rise to store peak flows. Big Creek WRF has inline flow equalization, as well as offline equalization for peak wet weather flows. Little River WRF lacks flow equalization at the plant but has some storage in the collection system.

To find the optimum balance, we will gradually and carefully lower the ammonia setpoint while monitoring mixed liquor filterability, an indicator of fouling potential.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **_Ultraviolet Disinfection_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
The plants have permit limits for bacterial indicators (fecal coliform and E. coli). These bacteria are larger than the pore size of the MBR membranes and are completely blocked if the membranes are intact. Usually, effluent limits for bacterial indicators can be met by an MBR process without downstream disinfection. However, many virus pass through the membrane pores, and this creates a human health risk not addressed by effluent limits for bacterial indicators. It is good practice to operate the downstream disinfection process to inactivate virus and to kill any bacteria present due to membrane damage. JC Solutions will always operate the UV disinfection process at its design dose to reduce the risk of pathogens on human health.

<!-- ¶7 -->
###### **_Solids Dewatering at JCEC and Big Creek_**

<!-- ¶8 -->
JCEC and Big Creek are similar in that they produce primary sludge (from primary clarifiers) and secondary sludge (from the MBR process). Both plants lack a thickening process other than what can be achieved in the primary clarifiers or by the membranes. Primary and secondary sludges are directed to aerated holding tanks/digesters, where the solids concentration decreases somewhat as digestion occurs.

<!-- ¶9 -->
Different dewatering technologies are used at these plants—centrifuges at JCEC ( **Exhibit 2-32** ) and screw presses at Big Creek. As a minimum, these dewatering processes must be operated so cake passes a paint filter test, which is a requirement for landfill disposal. Individual landfills may have additional requirements.

<!-- ¶10 -->
It is desirable to achieve cake with higher solids concentration, which reduces hauling and disposal costs. However, there are tradeoffs between cake concentration and the way primary and secondary treatment are

<!-- ¶11 -->
operated. Operating the primary clarifiers to produce thicker primary sludge tends to increase dewatered cake concentration, but it also decreases primary clarifier effluent quality, leading to cost increases in secondary treatment. Operating the MBR

<!-- ¶12 -->
Exhibit 2-32. _Centrifuges for solids dewatering at JCEC_

<!-- ¶13 -->
process to produce thicker secondary sludge would also tend to increase dewatered cake concentration, but as discussed above, it is desirable to use surface wasting to improve mixed liquor filterability and membrane performance.

<!-- ¶14 -->
###### ABOVE AND BEYOND

<!-- ¶15 -->

<!-- ¶16 -->
There is a delicate balance of competing factors, where operation for an advantage in part of the plant results in a disadvantage elsewhere in the plant. Our O&M staff and wastewater engineers are familiar with these trade-offs and will use process simulation and digital tools to find the balance that maximizes advantages and minimizes disadvantages.

<!-- ¶17 -->
**_How It Benefits Fulton County:_** _Potentially reduce costs as a result of improving cake dryness and lowering chemical consumption by intelligently managing sludge production and wasting practices._

<!-- ¶18 -->
###### **_Protection of Potable Water Supply_**

<!-- ¶19 -->
Drawings of Big Creek WRF show a double backflow preventer to isolate the potable water supply (1W) from plant reuse water (3W). This is not appropriate for a high hazard connection such as plant effluent. There is pressurized reuse water on the downstream side of the backflow preventers, and failure would result in contamination of the potable water supply. We will help the County determine whether a reverse pressure zone (RPZ) backflow preventer is required.

###### **_Biosolids Facilities Assessment: Key Findings_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
Our biosolids engineering team has conducted a comprehensive assessment of solids management requirements and operational challenges at the North Fulton facilities to develop a customized strategy for optimizing solids handling processes.

<!-- ¶7 -->
###### **_Big Creek WRF_**

<!-- ¶8 -->
Big Creek is under construction, with the aerobic digesters currently being built. Half of the dewatering capacity is inoperative due to a problem with one of the Schwing screw presses. Temporary dewatering is onsite. With one screw press inoperative, it appears that there is a need for temporary dewatering due to the presence of the mobile dewatering belt filter press. Many factors are probably responsible for this situation, and to anticipate every situation that could occur with the Schwing presses would not be possible; however, if screw press throughput is not adequately met with only one unit, then new plans should be considered for greater redundancy.

###### **ODOR AND NOISE MITIGATION**

<!-- ¶2 -->
JC Solutions recognizes the importance of odor control at the North Fulton facilities, especially given the residential, recreational, and commercial nature of adjacent areas. Significant investments in odor control have been made at all three sites, and particularly at Big Creek WRF and JCEC which cover most, if not all, processes to capture and treat odors from plant operations. This approach, however, is not bulletproof. Although Monthly Operating Reports show no odor complaints in 2024, the conditions for which the existing odor control facilities were designed may have changed (e.g., odor characteristics, meteorological conditions), and as such, opportunities may exist to improve the performance of existing systems. As part of our proactive approach to O&M, we are including a value-add to study odor mitigation strategies to ascertain effective odor mitigation.

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Odor and Noise Control Program_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
JC Solutions will routinely monitor the plants for odors including the presence of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and nuisance odors using a portable meter. Performance of the existing odor control facilities will also be monitored. Operators will make routine patrols of the plant and the boundary using both the portable meters as well as their own senses to determine if H2S or other odor conditions are detectable. Once per shift, JC Solutions will make an off-site patrol to specified potential odor source locations in neighboring vicinities during the known high odor season using a portable H2S meter. Any

<!-- ¶5 -->
detection of abnormal odor or H2S readings will be cause for JC Solutions to implement a corrective action plan. Written guidelines will be prepared for operators to follow if any of these elements are detected. JC Solutions will record each plant patrol finding, including any measured readings of noise, H2S, or detection of odor on an Odor Inspection Log. JC Solutions will sign the log for each patrol indicating time of patrol, weather conditions, wind speed, and direction.

<!-- ¶6 -->
Our project at the WWTP in Waterbury, CT, provides a successful example of Jacobs implementing an odor control mitigation strategy (illustrated in **Exhibit 2-36** ). We plan to apply the same methodology at the North Fulton facilities. We will start with JCEC and include an analysis of the performance of the exiting odor control facilities similar to **Exhibit 2-37** . The results of our Odor Emissions Study and our odor control mitigation strategy will be integrated into the O&M Plan for Process Control, focusing on properly operating scrubbers to avoid offsite odors.

We recognize that utility infrastructure requires a balanced security approach—one that protects critical systems without interrupting essential operations. Jacobs draws on extensive experience securing water and wastewater facilities nationwide. Our integrated approach pairs physical safeguards with utility-specific expertise to proactively mitigate risk and ensure service continuity.

<!-- ¶2 -->
By embedding a culture of safety and security into every aspect of operations, we will deliver a secure, compliant, and resilient environment that protects the County’s critical assets and the community they serve.

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Security Monitoring_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
Security monitoring plays a critical role in early detection and response to security threats. At utility sites, it functions as the “eyes and ears” of the operation, enabling rapid awareness of intrusions or unusual activity. JC Solutions will evaluate monitoring practices across key areas including perimeter security, facility access, fire alarm integration, physical and electronic access control systems, and sensitive in-building areas. Effective monitoring also contributes to employees’ safety by enabling timely emergency notifications and ensuring that intrusion detection systems are responsive and well-integrated. Our assessments will review how these elements work together to detect unauthorized access and support quick, coordinated responses to incidents.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **_Security Governance_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
Security governance provides the organizational framework for implementing and maintaining a successful security program. A strong governance model starts with leadership buy-in at all levels, from upper management to frontline staff, and includes the development and enforcement of policies and procedures that clearly define responsibilities during normal operations and during security events. In addition to policy development, we will evaluate the presence of training programs, employee awareness efforts, and administrative oversight to ensure a cohesive, system-wide security culture. This includes ensuring that daily operations, staff behavior, and equipment maintenance are guided by clearly defined standards and consistently reinforced expectations.

<!-- ¶7 -->
###### **_Security Technology_**

<!-- ¶8 -->
Technology supports both the monitoring and governance components of a security program by providing tools that increase visibility, improve access control, and ensure secure perimeters. We will also consider how well these systems support both daytime and nighttime security, and how they align with the facility’s operational needs. <!-- ¶21 -->
###### **CYBERSECURITY**

<!-- ¶22 -->
JC Solutions understands that cybersecurity is critical to the reliability and resilience of wastewater treatment operations. As cyber threats targeting water and wastewater utilities increase, our team will apply a proven and comprehensive strategy to safeguard Industrial Control Systems (ICS), SCADA, and business systems across the North Fulton Service Area.

<!-- ¶23 -->
Jacobs brings deep expertise in ICS cybersecurity, shaped by years of work with federal, municipal, and confidential clients—including the EPA. Our approach is aligned with NIST SP 800-series guidance and includes both proactive defense strategies and rapid response protocols to protect infrastructure, data, and public health. Using the Purdue model, assets are divided based on their criticality, and separate process areas are isolated to prevent lateral movement between systems. Security controls and network inspection are added between areas to monitor and manage access. Real-time monitoring is used to ensure that security controls are operable, and issues are detected before operations are impacted. Systems are kept patched and updated to ensure mitigation against the latest vulnerabilities.

<!-- ¶24 -->
Our cybersecurity program for the County will include:

<!-- ¶25 -->
- µ<sup>**Risk and resilience assessment**to identify cybersecurity risks and</sup> provide recommended mitigations.

<!-- ¶26 -->
- µ<sup>**Development of a site-specific cybersecurity and SCADA Security**</sup> **Plan** as part of our overall safety and risk management approach, as required by Article 50.8 and Exhibit 4 of the contract .

<!-- ¶27 -->
- µ<sup>**Implementation of ICS-focused cybersecurity policies and**</sup> **procedures** , including logical and physical network architecture reviews, remote access controls, endpoint protection, and penetration testing of WAN systems.

Many facilities and utilities do not have adequate backup systems in place. During our brief review of the core control systems for the wastewater facilities, it is unclear if the utility has an offsite backup system. We will implement an improved backup strategy following the 3-2-1-1 rule, including offsite and immutable cloud storage backups. This approach minimizes downtime and data loss in the unfortunate event of server failure or malicious attack.

<!-- ¶6 -->
A robust and thorough disaster recovery plan depends on complete and validated backups of all systems. Establishing a baseline backup of all systems will be the Operational Technology (OT) team’s highest priority in the first 90 Days. These backups will primarily be stored onsite, and immutable encrypted copies will be made offsite to ensure availability during a disaster. Combined with a robust emergency response plan, this will provide operational continuity even through the worst natural or man-made disasters.

<!-- ¶7 -->
We will also provide secure integration of SCADA, LIMS, CMMS, GIS, and other critical systems. Data will be stored and shared via encrypted, access-controlled systems that are fully auditable and aligned with both County IT protocols and Article 13 confidentiality requirements .

This cybersecurity framework, combined with Jacobs’ history of successfully defending client assets from sophisticated attacks, ensures secure and uninterrupted service delivery for the County’s wastewater facilities and pump stations.

###### **_Handling Public Concerns and Complaints_**

<!-- ¶24 -->
Because many of these neighborhoods already have a history with a nearby facility, developing and implementing a standard process to handle complaints about operations, especially odor, is critical to being a good neighbor. Working with operational staff, we will develop a complaint reporting system that gives residents and citizens a direct way to communicate concerns.

<!-- ¶25 -->
**Complaint Intake and Tracking.** We will provide a system for 24/7 odor complaint notification and response. We will maintain a record of the number of calls received and information on the odor complaints using a log form that will include, at a minimum, the following information:

<!-- ¶26 -->
- µ<sup>Name of Contractor’s employee that received the complaint</sup>

<!-- ¶27 -->
- µ<sup>Nature of complaint</sup>

<!-- ¶8 -->
**Response Protocol.** We will receive and acknowledge complaints as required. We will follow up each complaint with a full investigation and action plan, as required. Creating a rapid response team to investigate and address odor complaints as soon as they are reported supports transparency and credibility. There would be a feedback mechanism to ensure that residents feel heard and that their concerns are being addressed featuring a means to follow up with complainants and inform them of the actions taken, anticipated duration, and other relevant details.

<!-- ¶9 -->
**Reporting and Follow-Up.** Monthly summaries of all public complaints, including response actions and resolutions, will be submitted to the County. Follow-up communication with the complainant will be conducted to confirm satisfaction with the resolution.

<!-- ¶10 -->
To support facility operations, odor complaint data and locations could be analyzed to identify patterns and sources. This information could support targeted solutions and improve overall odor management in the event of ongoing or longer-term issues.

<!-- ¶11 -->
**Sludge or Biosolids Spills.** In the event of a spill impacting roadways or public spaces, emergency containment procedures will be activated, and local authorities will be notified. Spill updates will be communicated to the public through pre-approved channels.

<!-- ¶12 -->
**Noise Complaints.** We will minimize noise through sound-dampening technology and restrict noisy operations to designated hours. Should complaints arise, we will reassess equipment and processes and communicate mitigation steps to the affected parties.

###### 2.9 **TRANSITION PLAN WITH APPROACH AND TIMELINE OF ACTIVITIES NECESSARY TO ACHIEVE THE COMMENCEMENT DATE**

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Fluid Continuity: Enabling Uninterrupted Excellence in Water Services_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
A smooth transition with a detailed plan and a dedicated transition team is one of the first steps in a successful partnership between the County and JC Solutions. We have a thorough understanding of the County’s needs and expectations and have developed a plan to deliver a high level of service on day one. We leverage the expertise of our transition experts to develop an approach that is tailored to the specific needs of the project and client, supported by additional resources that will supplement the local team. This helps confirm transition activities occur in parallel while project tasks are seamlessly implemented. **Our transition plan described in this section reflects a highly organized process that couples our past experience transitioning operations with a focus on addressing specific project and client needs.** It efficiently organizes the local staff and provides sufficient qualified resources in all disciplines to assure the County of superior operations, maintenance, and administrative coverage for the managed assets. At the same time, this additional team of SMEs enables all Jacobs’ tools and strategies to be implemented at the project level without impacting the workload or effectiveness of the local team.

###### **_Thoughtful and Smooth Step-by-Step Transition Process for New Employees_**

<!-- ¶3 -->
While the physical process of the transition is hugely important, we view this step as more than a transfer of responsibilities from the County to us. **JC Solutions’ transition is the first step in the transformation of the County’s operations to a high-performing utility. One that is focused on leveraging the tools and capabilities of the larger Jacobs and driving ongoing improvement. As such, we invest significantly in the implementation of our systems, tools, and processes, coupled with a strong focus on training and the development of our culture.** The result is a high-performing local team that is engaged, empowered to deliver on all project needs, fully integrated into the region, and well equipped to leverage the strength of Jacobs’ technical capabilities.

<!-- ¶4 -->
Transition planning will start immediately after notification of award to allow SMEs and teams to assemble, organize, and prepare to address all aspects of the transition on the contract date. Nevertheless, our approach includes the integration of due diligence and transition resources so that even prior to award, our transition experts are already engaged in the project. A key aspect of our transition is to provide full transparency through open and frequent communications in a structure that will be adapted to the specific needs and expectations of the County.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **_Tapping the Value of Existing Staff_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
**We believe that the institutional knowledge of existing staff is a vital asset, and we are committed to offering competitive wages and benefits to qualified and interested candidates.** At JC Solutions, we recognize the knowledge and invaluable contributions of the employees currently working at the facility. **Our goal is to retain as many of these talented individuals as possible, leveraging their qualifications, capabilities, and the specific needs of the County.** Our commitment to local teams is evident in seamlessly transitioning over a dozen projects in the last three years, with a 90% conversion rate for qualified employees receiving job offers in the water sector's O&M services.

<!-- ¶7 -->
Our approach to building a strong team focuses on a blend of existing employees who will transition to JC Solutions, existing JC Solutions resources, and targeted recruitment efforts to fill any potential gaps. While unlikely, should only a limited number of current staff choose to join us, we will implement a comprehensive recruiting strategy that starts with leveraging existing JC Solutions employees and is supplemented externally, as detailed in our **_Long-term Staffing and Succession Planning Practices_** . To proactively address any staffing needs, we have identified several existing resources that would help us fill project roles and have initiated a focused pipeline search to identify local talent, so that we can fill any critical roles effectively. We also maintain a robust network of local providers who can support our team as necessary.

<!-- ¶8 -->
**During the transition phase, we will leverage our extensive regional and technical resources to temporarily fill any unexpected vacancies, ensuring that operations remain uninterrupted from day one.** This proactive strategy not only addresses unexpected staffing needs but also showcases the reliability and depth of JC Solutions' resources, reinforcing our commitment to seamless operations for the County. This approach also allows us to help the local team assimilate the strategies, tools, and the approach the team uses to deliver superior operations and provide a high-quality service.

<!-- ¶9 -->
Both existing and new employees will be supported with resources drawn from within JC Solutions. We will implement a proven six-step process to provide a high level of communication which in turn minimizes stress and results in a smooth workforce transition.

<!-- ¶1 -->
###### **_Exit Transition Plan_**

<!-- ¶2 -->
Although an Exit Transition Plan is something we hope will not be necessary, JC Solutions has developed a robust plan to ensure continuity of operations, seamless data and knowledge transfer, and accurate documentation. In accordance with Article 49 and Exhibit 6 of the Contract, JC Solutions will develop a detailed Exit Transition Plan within 90 days of the Commencement Date. This plan will outline all handback requirements and initiate transition activities no later than nine months prior to the end of the O&M term. The plan will ensure that all transition activities—including operational, technical, administrative, and regulatory elements—are coordinated to maintain service reliability and comply with all contract expectations.

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_JC Solutions’ Approach to the Exit Transition Process_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
JC Solutions’ approach to the exit transition process at the County emphasizes proactive planning, seamless knowledge transfer, clear documentation, and preservation of asset quality. While large-scale exit transitions are not common for Jacobs, our experience including recent transitions such as Coos Bay has informed key priorities and challenges, guiding us in developing robust processes to ensure an orderly, compliant, and thorough handover.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **_Comprehensive Exit Transition Strategy_**

<!-- ¶6 -->
JC Solutions’ Exit Transition Plan will align with all requirements outlined in the RFP, Exhibit 6, and Articles 6.6, 49, 50.6, and 53.2 of the Contract. Our plan includes detailed roles, responsibilities, and timelines to coordinate effectively with the County and any successor operator.

<!-- ¶7 -->
###### **_Key Elements of the Exit Transition Plan_**

<!-- ¶8 -->
**1. Documentation and Data Handover.** JC Solutions will provide the County with a complete set of updated management plans, operating manuals, and historical maintenance records. In compliance with Article 50.6 and 50.12, this includes:

<!-- ¶9 -->
- –A master inventory of all project-related records, including compliance reports, vendor invoices, operator logs, and laboratory data—indexed and converted into accessible electronic formats.

<!-- ¶10 -->
- –Identification and return or archival of proprietary Jacobs materials, clearly distinguished from County-owned documentation.

<!-- ¶11 -->
- –Complete transfer of regulatory documentation such as permits, inspection reports, and Discharge Monitoring Reports (DMRs), ensuring legal and regulatory compliance.

<!-- ¶12 -->
**2. Asset Condition and Inventory Management.** In accordance with Article 53.2, JC Solutions will conduct a thorough assessment of all facility assets and generate detailed condition reports. This will include:

<!-- ¶13 -->
- –Final inventory assessment of tools, equipment, spare parts, and consumables, with supporting documentation on all transfers or decommissioned items.

<!-- ¶14 -->
- –Verification and documentation of vehicles and equipment registration, transfer, or termination.

<!-- ¶15 -->
- –A comparison of final asset conditions to baseline records established at the project’s start, with recommendations for capital improvements where applicable.

<!-- ¶16 -->
**3. Staffing and Knowledge Transfer.** JC Solutions will provide comprehensive staffing data to support a smooth transition. As outlined in Article 6.6(B), the County or its successor operator will have the right to

<!-- ¶11 -->

<!-- ¶13 -->
As permitted by Article 6.6(C), JC Solutions is prepared to provide up to 180 days of extended support post-exit, at the County’s request, to ensure a smooth and professional handover.

<!-- ¶14 -->
**6. Proactive Risk Management.** We proactively address key transition risks such as service disruption, compliance gaps, and knowledge loss through:

<!-- ¶15 -->
- –Safety: Pre-handover safety audits and full protocol transfer.

<!-- ¶16 -->
- –Environment: Verified transfer of compliance data and updated permits.

<!-- ¶17 -->
- –Continuity: Operational readiness checks and inventory stock reviews.

<!-- ¶18 -->
- –Human Resources: Early coordination of interviews, training, and knowledge sharing.

<!-- ¶19 -->
###### **_Maintaining Exit Transition Readiness_**

<!-- ¶20 -->
JC Solutions will maintain transition readiness throughout the contract by conducting annual updates to the Exit Transition Plan. These updates will reflect operational changes, system upgrades, or new regulatory obligations, ensuring the final handover is always well-supported and executable with minimal disruption.

<!-- ¶21 -->
###### **_Lessons Learned_**

<!-- ¶22 -->
JC Solutions’ experience with exit transitions, such as Coos Bay, has highlighted the importance of early planning, thorough documentation, and proactive risk management. Structured communication protocols, detailed asset assessments, and collaborative planning with clients have proven key to success. These lessons will directly inform our approach at the County’s facilities, ensuring a seamless transition.

“The MBR treatment process is highly data-driven and requires continuous monitoring. Operators must be proactive, careful and diligent—MBRs aren’t as forgiving as a conventional activated sludge process. It’s a chemical process more than a biological process. Cleaning the membranes properly is key, as is managing the aeration system. Once the membranes get fouled, they can’t be recovered quickly.

<!-- ¶7 -->
The team’s ability to work with instrumentation and small mechanical components is important. Proper training is essential. Jacobs’ membrane technologists are really good—we pull them in all the time for advice or send them data to review. The membrane manufacturer will always point fingers elsewhere, so it’s great to have someone who can read the data and spot trends to help solve a problem.”

###### **JACOBS COLLECTION SYSTEM PUMP STATION EXPERIENCE**

<!-- ¶5 -->
Jacobs has extensive experience in the operation and maintenance of pump stations, providing comprehensive services that ensure the reliability and efficiency of water and wastewater systems. As one of the largest water and wastewater O&M service providers in North America, Jacobs manages pump stations for cities, counties, service jurisdictions, and industrial facilities. Our approach integrates advanced technologies and preventive maintenance practices to optimize equipment performance and minimize downtime. Jacobs' expertise includes pipeline condition assessments, asset management, and trenchless rehabilitation solutions, which are crucial for maintaining the integrity of pump stations and associated infrastructure.

<!-- ¶6 -->
Moreover, Jacobs' O&M services are tailored to meet the specific needs of each client, leveraging over four decades of successful delivery in the industry. We employ skilled staff and innovative solutions to address challenges such as leaks, corrosion, and wet weather management. By focusing on sustainability and adapting to changing environmental conditions, Jacobs ensures that pump stations operate efficiently and effectively, contributing to the overall resilience of conveyance systems. Our commitment to quality service and risk management helps clients reduce costs and improve service quality, making Jacobs a trusted partner in the operation and maintenance of pump stations.

Jacobs designed and built the Spokane County Regional Water Reclamation Facility (SCRWRF) and now operates and maintains the facilities. The 8.5-mgd facility is expandable to 24-mgd and uses state-of-theart membrane bioreactor and chemically enhanced primary treatment to reduce phosphorus levels in the effluent to less than 50 parts per billion (PPB).

<!-- ¶4 -->
Beginning in January 2009, Jacobs’ scope of work for the SCRWRF encompassed the design, permitting, construction, commissioning, and long‐term operations of the new treatment facility. Facilities constructed on the 20-acre site include:

<!-- ¶5 -->
In 1999, Spokane County Utilities began planning a new water reclamation facility when the City of Spokane decided that its existing facility would not have adequate capacity to serve the long-term regional wastewater treatment needs. Excessive phosphorus in the Spokane River was causing severe dissolved oxygen depletion in the Spokane River and Lake Spokane. Phosphorus and other nutrients, such as ammonia, encourage the growth of algae and other aquatic plants. When the plants decompose, they use up oxygen in the water, suffocating fish. After several years of planning, Spokane County Utilities selected Jacobs in 2008 to design, build, and operate a new treatment plant that will significantly reduce pollution going to the Spokane River and Lake Spokane.

<!-- ¶5 -->
Jacobs started up the facility approximately seven months ahead of schedule. The facility received its National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit on November 30, 2011, and effluent discharge to the Spokane River began on December 1, 2011. The facility additionally holds a permit for air quality from Spokane Regional Clean Air Agency. Additionally, the facility has remained in compliance, including through capital improvements and construction, with all effluent nutrient limits (50 PPB phosphorus and 0.25 PPM ammonia limits)—some of the most stringent limits in the nation, especially during summer months.

<!-- ¶6 -->
###### **_Accomplishment in Terms of Cost Savings, Capital, or Other Improvements Implemented_**

<!-- ¶7 -->
Jacobs conducts out-of-scope work to identify potential capacity improvements using models. We have already completed capital improvements to the influent screening, post-aerobic digester, and supplementary carbon systems. The facility was commissioned in 2011 and has since been under construction.

<!-- ¶8 -->
Due to a shortage of qualified local staff in the Spokane area, we’ve staffed the facility as leanly as possible. To ensure continued success, Jacobs has proactively supplemented the team by drawing on our deep bench of talent—including experienced operators from other projects, as well as regional technical and maintenance managers, compliance specialists, and safety professionals. This strategic support from across the company allows us to maintain high performance despite local staffing constraints.

<!-- ¶2 -->
The 3.1-mgd, $37-million reuse facility was implemented to fulfill the city’s growing population and provide highly treated recycled water. We saved the city more than $100,000 through value engineering.

<!-- ¶3 -->
###### **_Detailed Description of the Work of the Proponent on This Project_**

<!-- ¶4 -->
Jacobs provided facilities planning and engineering, design, construction, obtaining governmental approvals, permitting, acceptance testing, startup, O&M, and warranty for the WWTP reuse facility.

<!-- ¶5 -->
###### **RELEVANT EXPERIENCE**

<!-- ¶6 -->
The selected treatment included both MBR as well as Siemens’ Cannibal™ process. MBR is delivering the highest quality water and provides exceptional effluent quality, creates the least environmental impact by use of a small footprint, significantly reduces costs, and offers simplified expansion for future needs. In addition to MBR, Siemens’ Cannibal solids reduction process has been incorporated into the new facility. The Cannibal process greatly reduces solids production with consequent capital and operating cost savings. It virtually eliminates biosolids production, which eliminates the need for expensive dewatering and digestion equipment and associated costs.

<!-- ¶7 -->
###### **_Detailed description of the facilities operated_**

<!-- ¶8 -->
The Clovis Sewage Treatment/Water Reuse Facility (Clovis ST/WRF) was built in anticipation of the future needs of the City of Clovis community. Prior to its construction, the City of Clovis’s sewage was conveyed to the Fresno-Clovis Regional Wastewater Treatment Plant.

<!-- ¶9 -->
The Clovis ST/WRF is a California Title 22 Quality Treatment Facility with effluent suitable for discharge into the environment. The facility is a membrane bioreactor (MBR) system, using the Siemens Cannibal<sup>TM</sup> solids reduction process.

# Additional Digital Tools for Next Level Optimization
